record_type_quote: To test this hypothesis, this study first involved replicating a past finding in which religious people were more prone to perceive a face in everyday objects than less-religious people. However, the difference was not significant in the past study, although a small effect size was observed (Riekki et al., 2013). First, study participants recruited from Japan rated the face-likeness of everyday objects (Study 1A). To compare the results with people from Western cultures, as in Riekki and colleagues’ study (2013), the study was also conducted in the United States (Study 1B).

targets.outcome_quote: In sum, Study 1 was conducted to identify the relationship between religiosity and anthropomorphism of everyday objects. Complementing the previous study by Riekki et al. (2013), religiosity was found to be a significant predictor of the anthropomorphism (the effect was not significant in the previous study, although a small effect size was observed). Next, given the finding from the prior study was successfully replicated, the effect of being watched by the anthropomorphized object on decision to donate among religious people was tested in Study 2, which was the main purpose of this study.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The author explicitly judges the prior finding successfully replicated. This verdict governs despite the earlier nonsignificant face-likeness difference becoming significant. The new donation study is an extension, not a replication of a separate identified published finding.
